quote: geeigneten Modulsystem nimt, welches aus ganzen ganzzahligen Funktionen besteht.?[?] (Congruenzgruppe mit einer Veränderlichen.)
english: ...suitable module system, which consists of entire integral functions? (Congruence group with one variable.)
topic: The page ends a remark on congruence groups in one variable and then begins a proof that any finite group of linear transformations can be transformed so that its substitution coefficients are rational functions of roots of unity; the first attempted lemma is struck through.

triage.modern_statement: This cannot be pinned down with any confidence. The surviving words ask whether something holds when one 'takes a suitable module system consisting of entire integral functions', meaning an ideal of polynomials with integer coefficients, presumably in one variable (Z[x]). The parenthetical names this a 'congruence group in one variable'. One plausible reading is that Hilbert was asking whether a given (finite) group can be realized as a group of substitutions taken modulo such a polynomial ideal, a 'congruence group'. But the beginning of the sentence is on the previous page, so neither the object nor the property in question is known. The next item on the page is a different, well-defined claim: any finite group of linear transformations can be transformed so that its coefficients are rational functions of roots of unity, i.e. realized over a cyclotomic field. That is not the question being checked here.
triage.answered_by: Cannot be determined for the fragment itself. The theorem Hilbert begins proving right after it is known in sharp form: Maschke conjectured it around 1900, and Richard Brauer proved in 1945 (Amer. J. Math.) that every complex representation of a finite group is realizable over the field of g-th roots of unity, where g is the group order. He later improved this to the field of e-th roots of unity, where e is the exponent. This is context only, not an answer to the fragmentary question.

evidence.claim: Maschke conjectured around 1900 that every representation of a group of exponent e is defined over Q(e-th roots of unity), and Brauer proved it in 1945 ('On the representation of a group of order g in the field of the g-th roots of unity').
Brauer proved that every complex representation of a finite group G is equivalent to one over the field of |G|-th roots of unity, and later improved this to the exponent of G.

In Hilbert's own usage, 'ganzzahlige Funktion' means an entire rational function (a polynomial) whose coefficients are rational integers. This supports reading 'module system of entire integral functions' as an ideal of polynomials with integer coefficients.

triage.why: The note is only the tail end of a sentence that started on the previous page. What survives says that something should hold modulo a suitable ideal of integer-coefficient polynomials, under the heading 'congruence group in one variable'. Without the subject of the sentence, the question cannot be stated precisely or matched to any published problem or later result. My searches found nothing linking a Hilbert problem or a known result to this wording. It is not one of the 23 problems or the 24th problem. The neighbouring cyclotomic-realization claim was settled by Brauer (1945), but treating that as the answer to this fragment would be speculation.
